title: The bee
hook: your Lord inspired the bee to build, to eat, to make honey with healing in it (16:68–69)

segments.voice: Yesterday: milk between, pure milk from between waste and blood. Your line was pure from between. Did you find one good thing that grew out of a mess? Day four hundred fifty-three.

A single bee, in its whole life, makes a very small amount of honey. A jar on your shelf is the work of a crowd you'll never meet, flying back and forth over fields you'll never see. This surah, number sixteen, is named after that crowd. An-Nahl: the Bee. Of all the creatures in its long list of gifts, the bee is the one that gets the name on the cover, and two verses all its own. Today, those two verses.

Verse sixty-eight begins, in Pickthall's words: "And thy Lord inspired the bee". The verb is awha, from the same root as wahy, the word for revelation. It's the word used when God speaks to prophets. It's also used, elsewhere in the Qur'an, for the quiet prompting given to the mother of Musa. And here it's used for an insect. Commentators usually explain it as instinct, a guidance placed inside the creature, but they keep the word: the bee is guided. Then come three instructions. Make your homes in the hills, in the trees, and in what people build for you. Eat from every kind of fruit. And follow the ways of your Lord, made smooth for you. Arabic grammarians have long pointed out that these commands are in the feminine form. Then verse sixty-nine: from their bellies comes "a drink diverse of hues, wherein is healing for mankind." Diverse of hues: anyone who's seen pale clover honey next to dark buckwheat knows it. Healing for people. The verse ends: this is a sign for people who reflect. There's a story in Sahih al-Bukhari that shows how seriously the companions took it. A man came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and said his brother's stomach was troubling him. Give him honey, the Prophet said. The man came back: no better. Honey, again. Back again, no better. The third time the Prophet said, God has spoken the truth and your brother's stomach is wrong; give him honey. He did, and his brother recovered. Muslims read the verse as a sign, and many also keep honey in the kitchen for sore throats. The verse names it a healing, not the only one.
screen: `AWHA: THE BEE IS GUIDED.` · `BUILD, EAT, FOLLOW THE SMOOTH WAYS.` · `A DRINK OF MANY COLORS.` · `HONEY, AGAIN, AND AGAIN.` · then, large: `WHEREIN IS HEALING FOR MANKIND.`

segments.voice: If you have honey in the house, put a little on a spoon. If you don't, anything sweet will do, or just remember the taste. Before it touches your tongue, look at its color, and picture the bees that crossed the fields to make it. Taste it slowly. Let it sit. Then, for the rest of the sit, think of one thing in your life that heals you: a person, a walk, a song, a habit. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for it. The bell holds the time.
The bee. Guided by the same word as revelation, told to build, eat and follow smooth paths, and giving a drink of many colors with healing in it. Today's word.
Your line: healing in it. Today, notice one small thing that does you good, a cup of tea, a friend's voice, ten minutes outside, and let yourself receive it fully. Day four hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Many Muslim households keep honey as a remedy and cite 16:69 and the hadith of the man with the stomach complaint; the bee verses are often recited and taught to children as a sign in creation.

awha and wahy: the same root, used for prophets, for Musa's mother, and here for the bee.

trapdoor: what you thought: honey is good for you, says a nice verse.
what it means: the bee is guided by God, and its drink of many colors carries healing as a sign for people who reflect.
what a scholar hears: awha is the verb of revelation, applied to an insect; commentators read it as instinct placed by God, and grammarians note the feminine commands.
